pages.text: On Cultural Day at school, Klenam played a tall wooden drum. Boom, boom, boom! “How does a drum make a sound?” asked Mame. “It is only stretched skin and carved wood.”
sentences: On Cultural Day at school, Klenam played a tall wooden drum.
Boom, boom, boom!
“How does a drum make a sound?” asked Mame.
“It is only stretched skin and carved wood.”
pages.alt: In a festive sunlit Ghanaian school courtyard, Klenam taps a tall carved wooden drum with a stick while Mame watches curiously.

pages.text: Their teacher smiled and said, “Place your fingers lightly near the edge of the drum skin while Klenam taps gently.” Mame felt a lively tickle under her fingertips. “It is shaking!” she cried. “That fast shaking is called vibration,” said the teacher.
sentences: Their teacher smiled and said, “Place your fingers lightly near the edge of the drum skin while Klenam taps gently.” Mame felt a lively tickle under her fingertips.
“It is shaking!” she cried.
“That fast shaking is called vibration,” said the teacher.
pages.alt: Mame resting her fingertips lightly on the stretched drumhead with a delighted smile as Klenam taps gently and their teacher watches.

pages.text: Next, Mame sprinkled a few uncooked grains of white rice onto the drum skin. Klenam tapped the drum again, and the tiny grains leaped and danced! “The drum skin is shaking so fast that the rice jumps!” said Klenam.
sentences: Next, Mame sprinkled a few uncooked grains of white rice onto the drum skin.
Klenam tapped the drum again, and the tiny grains leaped and danced!
“The drum skin is shaking so fast that the rice jumps!” said Klenam.
pages.alt: Close view of the stretched wooden drumhead as white rice grains bounce and hop in the air when Klenam taps the drum beside Mame.

pages.text: Then their teacher laid her open palm flat across the drum skin to stop the shaking. At once, the sound stopped too, and the rice lay still. “No shaking means no sound,” she explained. “Every sound is made by something vibrating.”
sentences: Then their teacher laid her open palm flat across the drum skin to stop the shaking.
At once, the sound stopped too, and the rice lay still.
“No shaking means no sound,” she explained.
“Every sound is made by something vibrating.”
pages.alt: Their teacher resting her flat palm gently on the drumhead so the white rice grains sit completely still while Klenam and Mame watch closely.

pages.text: “The vibrating drum skin makes the air around it shake too,” continued the teacher. “That shaking air travels all the way to our ears, and that is how we hear.” Mame grinned. “So the drum talks to the air, and the air talks to us!”
sentences: “The vibrating drum skin makes the air around it shake too,” continued the teacher.
“That shaking air travels all the way to our ears, and that is how we hear.” Mame grinned.
“So the drum talks to the air, and the air talks to us!”
pages.alt: Beside the carved wooden drum, the teacher cups one hand gently near her ear as Mame smiles brightly and Klenam listens.

pages.text: Their teacher shared a helpful safety rule as well. “Very loud sounds can hurt our ears. We play instruments at a safe volume, and we step back whenever a noise is too loud.” Klenam tapped softly, and the rice danced a gentle dance.
sentences: Their teacher shared a helpful safety rule as well.
“Very loud sounds can hurt our ears.
We play instruments at a safe volume, and we step back whenever a noise is too loud.” Klenam tapped softly, and the rice danced a gentle dance.
pages.alt: Klenam tapping the wooden drum softly in the sunny courtyard while the white rice grains hop gently and Mame listens happily.

activities.question: Why did the grains of rice jump on the drum?
options: The drum skin was shaking fast

activities.question: What happened as soon as the teacher rested her palm on the drum skin?
options: The shaking and the sound stopped
